stem: Two engineers at the same firm earn the same salary. Faisal saves 18% of his and Nawaf saves 12% of his. Faisal saves 1440 SAR a month. How much does Nawaf save, in SAR?
trick: one per cent of the shared salary is the bridge — never work out the salary itself
why: 1% of the salary is 1440 ÷ 18 = 80 SAR, so 12% is 80 × 12 = 960 SAR. (The salary is 8000, but you never have to write it down.)
traps: A: halved 1440 on the grounds that 12 is roughly half of 18.
B: scaled by 12/18 but rounded 80 down to 70.
D: scaled by 18/12 instead of 12/18.

stem: A survey counted the visitors to two heritage sites in one season, shown below. Find the ratio of the first to the second.
trick: the power of ten is the same on both sides, so it cancels and never enters the arithmetic
traps: A: wrote the ratio the wrong way round.
C: divided 6 by 1.5 as though 1.5 were 1.
D: used the difference 4.5 × 10⁵ instead of the quotient.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: 180% means multiply by 1.8, so K is SMALLER than 3600, not larger
why: 1.8K = 3600 gives K = 2000, which is less than 2200, so B is greater.
traps: A: read the statement as 'K is 180% more than 3600' and got 6480.
C: guessed that a comparison item must balance.
D: K is fully determined by the statement.

stem: Which quantity is greater?   A: 380   B: 40% of 900
trick: work the percentage out in full — 40% of 900 is close enough to 380 that estimating will not settle it
why: 40% of 900 is 360, and 380 > 360, so A is greater.
traps: B: read 40% of 900 as 400 by taking 'a bit under a half' too generously.
C: rounded 360 up to 380 and called it a tie.
D: both quantities are fully given, so 'not enough information' cannot apply.

stem: On Tuesday 21 students were present in a class and 30% of the class was absent. How many students are in the class altogether?
trick: the 21 who came are the 70% who were NOT absent, so divide by 0.7, not by 0.3
why: If 30% were absent then 70% attended, and that 70% is 21 students. So the class is 21 ÷ 0.70 = 30.
traps: A: divided 21 by 0.84 after a slip.
C: took 21 as 30% and divided by 0.3 — the word ABSENT was missed.
D: divided 21 by 0.3.

stem: A supplier delivers 8 water coolers for 640 SAR. What does it cost to deliver 14 coolers, at the same rate?
trick: unit price first, then multiply — one division and one multiplication, never a guessed jump
why: One cooler costs 640 ÷ 8 = 80 SAR, so 14 cost 80 × 14 = 1120 SAR.
traps: A: scaled by 12/8 instead of 14/8.
B: added 380 for the six extra at a guessed rate.
D: doubled 640.

stem: An empty storage tank weighs 420 kg. Filled to one fifth of its capacity it weighs 620 kg. What does it weigh when it is three fifths full?
trick: subtract the empty weight before scaling the water, never after
why: One fifth of the water weighs 620 − 420 = 200 kg, so three fifths weigh 600 kg. The tank still weighs 420 kg, giving 420 + 600 = 1020 kg.
traps: B: added 700 instead of 600 by scaling from 620 ÷ 3.
C: used 620 + 620 for the extra two fifths.
D: tripled the whole 620 kg — the empty weight must come off first.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: simplify B fully — a comparison can be a disguised identity
why: B is 12√20 ÷ (4√4) = 12 × 2√5 ÷ 8 = 24√5 ÷ 8 = 3√5, which is exactly A. They are equal.
traps: A: stopped at 12 ÷ 4 = 3 and never simplified √20 or √4.
B: took √20 as 2√10.
D: both are explicit numbers, so 'not enough information' cannot apply.

stem: A number is a multiple of 8. Six less than it is a multiple of 7. Which of the following is the number?
trick: test the options against BOTH conditions; one condition alone leaves all four standing
why: All four are multiples of 8. Subtracting 6: 34, 42, 50, 58. Only 42 is a multiple of 7, so the number is 48.
traps: A: 40 − 6 = 34, not a multiple of 7.
C: 56 is itself a multiple of 7, which is not the condition asked for.

stem: Solve for t.
trick: dividing by a negative exponent ADDS, so the two sevenths make a whole t
why: 2/7 + 5/7 = 1, so the bracket is t. Then t × t³ = t⁴ = 16, giving t = 2.
traps: B: subtracted the exponents and solved t³ = 16 badly.
C: solved t² = 16.
D: read t⁴ = 16 as t = 16.

stem: Take away as little as possible from 1000 so that what is left divides exactly by 43. How much is taken away?
trick: the remainder on division IS the number to subtract
why: 43 × 23 = 989, and 1000 − 989 = 11, so the remainder is 11 and 11 must come off.
traps: A: used 991 as the nearest multiple, which is not one.
C: divided by 41 rather than 43.
D: took 983 as the target by subtracting a whole extra 6.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: round 63.98 to 64 and 1.001 to 1 — the estimate settles it without any long division
why: 0.25 × 64 = 16, and 16 ÷ 1 = 16. The true value is 15.98, which is still greater than 15, so A is greater.
traps: B: divided by 1.001 as though it were 1.1, giving about 14.5.
C: rounded 15.98 to 16 and then to 15.
D: every number is given, so the comparison is decidable.

stem: A courtyard 36 m by 60 m is to be paved exactly with identical square slabs. What is the largest possible side of one slab, in metres?
trick: 'largest square that tiles it exactly' is the HCF of the two sides
why: The side must divide both 36 and 60, so the largest is HCF(36, 60) = 12 m.
traps: A: gave a common factor, but not the largest.
B: 9 divides 36 but not 60.
D: 18 divides 36 but not 60.

stem: The number below is divisible by n. Which of these can n be?
trick: a power of 3 has only threes in it, so any divisor must also be a pure power of 3
why: 3¹² has only the prime factor 3, so any divisor is a power of 3. Of the options only 27 = 3³ qualifies; 15, 18 and 24 each carry a 2 or a 5.
traps: A: 15 = 3 × 5 — the factor 5 is not present.
B: 18 = 2 × 9 — the factor 2 is not present.
C: 24 = 8 × 3 — the factor 8 is not present.

stem: Only one of the four numbers below is prime. Which one?
trick: check 3 and 7 before deciding — 51, 57 and 91 all look prime and none of them is
why: 67 is not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7, and 8² = 64 < 67 < 81, so testing to 7 is enough. 51 = 3 × 17, 57 = 3 × 19, 91 = 7 × 13.
traps: A: 51 is odd, but 5 + 1 = 6 is a multiple of 3.
B: 57 is odd, but 5 + 7 = 12 is a multiple of 3.
D: 91 looks prime and is 7 × 13 — the classic trap.

stem: Complete the sequence: 3, 3, 6, 18, …
trick: the multipliers run 1, 2, 3, 4 — the differences do not form the pattern
traps: A: doubled 18.
B: multiplied by 3 again instead of moving on to 4.
D: extended the differences (0, 3, 12) rather than the multipliers.

stem: Find the quotient.
trick: check the last digit: 372 ends in 2, so only a quotient ending in 3 can give a dividend ending in 6
why: 372 × 173 203 = 64 431 516. The units digit settles it without any long division: 2 × 3 = 6, and no other option ends in a digit that gives 6.
traps: A: 2 × 1 ends in 2, not 6.
C: 2 × 4 ends in 8.
D: 2 × 7 ends in 4.

stem: Rakan has 48 banknotes. One sixth of them are 10 SAR notes and one quarter are 50 SAR notes. The rest are 100 SAR notes. How much does Rakan have altogether, in SAR?
trick: the 'rest' is what is left after BOTH fractions, not after one of them
why: One sixth of 48 is 8 ten-riyal notes (80 SAR); one quarter is 12 fifty-riyal notes (600 SAR); the rest is 48 − 8 − 12 = 28 hundred-riyal notes (2800 SAR). The total is 80 + 600 + 2800 = 3480 SAR.
traps: B: used 29 hundred-riyal notes.
C: took the 'rest' as 48 − 12 = 36, forgetting the ten-riyal notes.
D: used 32 hundred-riyal notes.

stem: A school of 480 students sent 35% of them on a field trip to Diriyah. How many students went?
trick: 10% first, then scale — 35% is three tens and a half-ten
traps: A: gave 30% and stopped.
C: gave 40%.
D: gave 45%.

stem: What is the next number in the sequence 8, 11, 17, 26, …?
trick: the differences run 3, 6, 9, so the next difference is 12
why: The differences are 3, 6, 9 — going up in threes — so the next difference is 12 and the term is 26 + 12 = 38.
traps: A: kept the difference at 9.
C: used a difference of 14.
D: doubled the last difference to 18.

stem: Find the number that, when multiplied by 8, equals 20% of 360.
trick: take the percentage first: 20% of 360 is 72, and only then divide
traps: A: used 20% of 280.
C: found 72 correctly but divided by 6.
D: divided 360 by 20 and stopped.

stem: Evaluate the expression below.
trick: dividing by a fraction flips it — the root of five cancels top and bottom before any arithmetic
why: The numerator is √5 × 6√3 = 6√15. Dividing by √5 ⁄ (3√3) means multiplying by 3√3 ⁄ √5, so the √5 cancels: 6√3 × 3√3 = 18 × 3 = 54.
traps: A: added the surds in the bracket as 2√3 + 4√3 = 6 and lost the root.
B: multiplied by √5 ⁄ (3√3) instead of dividing by it.
D: squared the 3 as well as the √3.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: 0.8% is eight tenths of one per cent, not eight per cent — convert both to plain numbers first
traps: A: read 0.8% as 8%, giving 720 — which would make B the larger anyway.
B: read 15% of 480 as 60.
D: both are explicit numbers.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: both differences are negative, so the one NEARER to zero is the greater
traps: B: compared 1/2 with 4/5 and picked the bigger number, ignoring the minus signs.
C: subtracted 9/10 from both and assumed that cancels the difference.
D: every number is given.

stem: A box of pens was shared among 14 students so that each received 18 pens, and 7 pens were left over. How many pens were in the box?
trick: multiply first, then ADD the leftover — the remainder is not part of the shares
traps: A: subtracted the leftover instead of adding it.
B: forgot the leftover altogether.
D: added 14 rather than 7.

stem: A school assigns 3 supervisors for every 25 pupils on a trip. If 400 pupils go, how many supervisors are needed?
trick: count the GROUPS first, then multiply — do not scale the two numbers separately
why: 400 ÷ 25 = 16 groups, and 16 × 3 = 48 supervisors.
traps: A: used 12 groups.
B: divided 400 by 28 (the group total) instead of by 25.
D: rounded 16 groups up to 17 and then some.

stem: Find the value of the expression below.
trick: 'of' means multiply, and a per cent sign is a division by 100 that is easy to drop
traps: B: dropped one factor of 10 by reading 0.05% as 0.5%.
C: read 0.05% as 5%.
D: treated both 0.05% and 0.02 as whole per cents.

stem: Find the value of the sum below.
trick: convert each fraction by its OWN denominator — the three place values are all different
traps: A: divided the whole answer by ten by lining the decimal points up wrongly.
D: transposed two digits after adding correctly.

stem: Calculate the value of the expression below.
trick: take the common factor out of the numerator first — no long multiplication is needed
traps: B: used 35(−18 + 11) ÷ 7 with the 35 mistaken for 25.
C: dropped the minus sign.
D: dropped the minus sign after the correct magnitude.

stem: Zero is excluded from both lists. Which is greater?   A: the product of the integers from −3 to 5   B: the product of the integers from −5 to 3
trick: split each product into its negative part and its positive part — the two lists turn out to be mirror images
traps: A: counted three negatives in A and five in B and concluded the signs differ — both products are in fact negative.
B: noticed that B reaches −5 and assumed the larger negative wins.
D: both lists are fully specified, so both products are determined.

stem: The whole numbers from 1 to 25 are written out. Which is greater?   A: the sum of the odd numbers among them   B: the sum of the even numbers among them
trick: there is one more odd number than even, and the odd list starts lower but reaches higher
why: The odd numbers 1, 3, …, 25 are 13 terms summing to 13² = 169. The even numbers 2, 4, …, 24 are 12 terms summing to 12 × 13 = 156. A is greater.
traps: B: assumed the evens win because each even is bigger than the odd before it.
C: assumed the two halves must balance.
D: both sums are fully determined.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: two conditions can force a case split — when the cases disagree, (D) is the answer
why: Substituting k = ab into ak = b gives a²b = b, so b(a² − 1) = 0. Either b = 0, or a = 1, or a = −1. Take a = 1: then k = b and b − a = b − 1, so A is greater. Take b = 0: then k = 0 and b − a = −a, whose sign depends on a. Different legitimate cases give different answers.
traps: A: found the a = 1 case and stopped there.
B: found a case where b − a is large and stopped there.
C: cancelled b from a²b = b without noting that b may be zero.

stem: Adding 3 to a number and then squaring the result gives 121. What is the number?
trick: a square root has two signs, but only one of them is on the option list
why: k + 3 = ±11, so k = 8 or k = −14. Only 8 appears among the options.
traps: B: took the square root of 121 and stopped, forgetting the +3.
C: added 3 to 11 instead of subtracting.
D: added 3 twice to 11.

stem: Find a possible pair of values of a and b.
trick: clear the common denominator first: the equation is simply a + b = 90
why: Multiplying through by 5 gives a + b = 90. Of the four pairs only 35 + 55 = 90.
traps: C: 40 + 45 = 85 — five short.
D: 50 + 60 = 110 — overshot by treating 18 as 22.

stem: A library lent out 14 of its copies of a title, then received 5 new copies, which left 43 copies on the shelf. How many copies were on the shelf to begin with?
trick: 'lent out' and 'received' move in opposite directions — work backwards and net them
why: If it started with n, then n − 14 + 5 = 43, so n − 9 = 43 and n = 52.
traps: A: mis-signed both movements, giving 43 − 5 − 4.
B: netted the two movements to zero.
D: added both movements instead of netting them (43 + 14 + 5).

stem: Evaluate the expression below.
trick: a negative cubed stays negative; the squared term is positive BEFORE the minus sign hits it
traps: B: took (−2)² as −4, giving −24 + 8 − 10 = −26 and then mis-added.
C: took (−2)² as −4.
D: dropped the −2w² term.

stem: Given the two equations below, find x + y + z.
trick: you are asked for the SUM, not for the letters — the y terms cancel and the sum is a constant
why: From the first, x = 10 − y/4. From the second, z = 18 − 3y/4. Adding: x + y + z = 10 − y/4 + y + 18 − 3y/4 = 28, because −1/4 + 1 − 3/4 = 0. The sum is 28 whatever y is.
traps: A: solved for one letter only and stopped.
B: assumed y = 0 and then dropped a term.
D: added 40 and 24 and halved.

stem: A number plus four times itself, increased by 9, is seven times the original number. Find the number.
trick: 'plus four times itself' is 5n, not 4n
why: n + 4n + 9 = 7n gives 5n + 9 = 7n, so 2n = 9 and n = 4.5.
traps: A: solved 4n + 9 = 7n, dropping the original n.
C: solved 5n + 9 = 6.5n after mis-reading 'seven times'.
D: gave the 9 that appears in the question.

stem: Find v.
trick: the nines on the two denominators cancel, leaving 7 = 0.7v
why: The denominators are both 9, so 7 = 0.7v and v = 10.
traps: A: inverted, giving 0.7 ÷ 7.
B: divided 7 by 7 and forgot the decimal.
D: multiplied by 10 twice.

stem: One grocery bill lists 4 kg of dates with 6 kg of rice at 300 SAR. A second lists 8 kg of dates with 4 kg of coffee at 600 SAR. Which is greater?   A: one kilogram of rice   B: one kilogram of coffee
trick: halve the second equation so both carry the same number of date units, then the rest subtracts away
why: Halving the second gives 4 dates + 2 coffee = 300. The first says 4 dates + 6 rice = 300. So 2 coffee = 6 rice, that is 1 coffee = 3 rice, and coffee is the greater.
traps: A: compared the coefficients 6 and 4 rather than the prices.
C: saw 300 and 600 as a clean doubling and assumed a tie.
D: the date terms cancel exactly, so the comparison IS decidable.

stem: Which quantity is greater, given the two statements below?
trick: solve for p and q first; 4p and 3q are then plain numbers
why: 5^p = 125 gives p = 3, so 4p = 12. 9q = 54 gives q = 6, so 3q = 18. B is greater.
traps: A: read 5^p = 125 as p = 5 and got 4p = 20.
C: solved 9q = 54 as q = 4, which would make both sides 12.
D: both letters are fully determined.

stem: Which quantity is greater, given the inequality below?
trick: solve the inequality first: h is above minus three quarters, and minus five sixths is below that
why: 3 + 4h > 0 gives h > −3/4. Since −3/4 = −0.75 and −5/6 ≈ −0.833, every allowed h is greater than −5/6. A is greater.
traps: B: solved the inequality the wrong way round to h < −3/4.
C: compared −3/4 with −5/6 and read them as equal.
D: the inequality bounds h above −5/6 for every allowed value.

stem: Which quantity is greater, given the equation below?
trick: no sign is given for either letter, and both may be zero, so no comparison can be made
why: 7u = 3v fixes the ratio but not the sign. If v = 7 then u = 3 and B is greater; if v = −7 then u = −3 and A is greater; if v = 0 then both are zero. Not enough information.
traps: A: assumed both letters are positive because 7 > 3.
B: read the equation as u = 3v/7 and compared the coefficients.
C: took the equals sign to mean the letters are equal.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: taking reciprocals only reverses an inequality when both sides carry the SAME sign, and no sign is given here
why: If g and n are both positive then g < n gives 1/g > 1/n, so A. But take g = −1 and n = 1: then g < n still holds, while 1/g = −1 and 1/n = 1, so B. Not enough information.
traps: A: applied 'reciprocals reverse the inequality' without checking the signs — this is the trap the item is built on.
B: found the mixed-sign case and stopped there.
C: assumed the reciprocals must balance.

stem: Which quantity is greater, given the two statements below?
trick: u + v = 0 makes v the opposite of u, so u − v is just 2u — and then compare two negatives
why: u + v = 0 gives v = 1/5, so u − v = −1/5 − 1/5 = −2/5. And 7u = −7/5. Since −2/5 > −7/5, A is greater.
traps: B: compared magnitudes and picked 7/5 as the bigger, ignoring the signs.
C: took u − v as 0 by confusing it with u + v.
D: both quantities are fully determined by u.

stem: A two-digit number has one digit greater than the other by 4, and its two digits add to 12. What is the number?
trick: the two conditions fix the digits before you look at the options; then only the ORDER is left to check
why: Digits differing by 4 and summing to 12 are 8 and 4. Of the options only 84 uses that pair.
traps: A: 3 + 9 = 12 but the digits differ by 6.
B: 5 + 7 = 12 but the digits differ by 2.
C: 6 + 6 = 12 but the digits do not differ at all.

stem: A canteen prices sandwiches at 8 SAR and juices at 5 SAR. Nasser takes at least one of each and hands over exactly 52 SAR. How many juices does he take?
trick: test the juice count, not the sandwich count — only one value leaves a multiple of 8
why: 8s + 5j = 52. Trying j = 4 gives 20, leaving 32, which is exactly 4 sandwiches. No other value of j under 10 leaves a multiple of 8.
traps: A: 2 juices leaves 42, not a multiple of 8.
C: 6 juices leaves 22.
D: 8 juices leaves 12.

stem: Given the two statements below, which of the following is INCORRECT?
trick: substitute r = 2p once and read all four options off it — three of them collapse to true statements immediately
why: Since p = q, r = p + q = 2p. Then (A) p = r⁄2 is true; (B) adding the same r to two equal quantities is true; (C) tripling p + q = r is true; (D) r − q = 2p − p = p, not 3p, so (D) is the incorrect one.
traps: A: r = 2p makes p = r⁄2 exactly.
B: adding the same amount to two equal quantities always holds.
C: this is the original equation multiplied through by 3.

stem: A number is multiplied by 24 and then 83 is subtracted. The result is 1069. What is the number?
trick: work backwards: undo the subtraction first, then the multiplication
traps: A: divided 1069 by 24 and rounded up.
B: subtracted 83 instead of adding it, then divided.
D: divided by 22.

stem: Given the two statements below, find c² + d².
trick: square the sum and subtract twice the product — you never need c and d themselves
traps: A: subtracted 14 twice more than needed.
C: subtracted only one lot of 14.
D: gave (c + d)² and forgot to subtract 2cd.

stem: The midpoints of the sides of the equilateral triangle below are joined, and the median from the apex is drawn. Find the area of the shaded triangle.
trick: join the midpoints, then halve again — the shaded piece is an eighth of the whole, and the area of an equilateral triangle is (root 3 over 4) times the side squared
why: The whole triangle has area (√3⁄4) × 16² = 64√3. Joining the midpoints cuts it into four congruent triangles, and the shaded piece is half of one of them — an eighth of the whole. So 64√3 ÷ 8 = 8√3.
traps: A: took a sixteenth by halving one step too many.
C: gave one of the four medial triangles, 64√3 ÷ 4, without the final halving.
D: gave half the whole triangle.

stem: The two triangles below are similar and drawn in the same orientation. Find the value of x.
trick: similar triangles share all three angles, so the third one is 180 minus the other two
why: Similar triangles have the same three angles: 35°, 60° and the apex. The apex is 180 − 35 − 60 = 85°, and x marks that apex.
traps: A: subtracted 35 from 110.
D: added the two given angles and subtracted from 200.

stem: In triangle KLM, P is the midpoint of KL and Q is the midpoint of KP. Find the ratio of KQ to KL.
trick: halving twice quarters the length — and read carefully WHICH two points the ratio is between
why: KP is half of KL, and KQ is half of KP, so KQ is a quarter of KL. (Both points lie on the same side, KL, which is what makes the ratio well defined.)
traps: B: halved once and stopped at the first midpoint.
C: no midpoint route gives a third.
D: took the remaining part, QL ⁄ KL = 3/4, instead of the part asked for.

stem: Six identical small rectangles make up the rectangle drawn below, whose perimeter measures 34 cm. What is the area of one small rectangle, in cm²?
trick: the perimeter gives the missing side; the height is already on the diagram
why: The height is 5 cm, so 2(L + 5) = 34 gives L = 12 cm. The whole area is 12 × 5 = 60 cm², and one of six equal parts is 60 ÷ 6 = 10 cm².
traps: A: used L = 12 but divided the area by 7.5 after a slip.
C: took L = 14 by forgetting that the perimeter counts each side twice.
D: divided 60 by 4.

stem: A triangle has the three sides listed below. A rectangle 6 cm wide covers exactly the same area as that triangle. What is the rectangle's perimeter, in cm?
trick: 9-12-15 is a right triangle, so its area is half the product of the two SHORT sides — the 15 never enters
why: 9² + 12² = 81 + 144 = 225 = 15², so the triangle is right-angled and its area is ½ × 9 × 12 = 54 cm². The rectangle has area 54 and width 6, so its length is 9 and its perimeter is 2(9 + 6) = 30 cm.
traps: B: used the triangle's own perimeter of 36.
C: added the length and width of the rectangle to the triangle's short sides.
D: gave the area rather than the perimeter.

stem: In the diagram below, O is the centre of the circle. Each shaded piece is bounded by three lines: the horizontal diameter, a second line through O drawn at 135° to it, and the tangent to the circle at the point where the diameter meets it. Find the total shaded area, in cm².
trick: the two pieces are right triangles with both legs equal to the radius, so together they come to exactly r squared
why: The line leaves O at 45° to the diameter, so each shaded piece is a right triangle with legs r and r. Each has area ½ × 25 = 12.5, and the two together give 25 cm².
traps: A: used ½ × r × r once and then rounded.
C: forgot to halve, giving r² × 2.
D: used the square on the diameter.

stem: In the circle below, two straight lines pass through the centre O. Which is greater?   A: arc PQR   B: arc PST
trick: both lines pass through the centre, so each arc is measured by its own central angle
why: Both lines are diameters, so each arc is measured by its central angle. The angle between them is 74°, so arc PQR = 74° and arc PST = 180 − 74 = 106°. B is the longer arc.
traps: A: read the 74° as belonging to the arc through S.
C: assumed two diameters always cut the circle into equal arcs.
D: the central angle is given, so both arcs are determined.

stem: In the figure, r and s are the midpoints of pv and qw. Also tv = uw = ¼ of rt = ¼ of su. Find the ratio of (rt + tv + su) to (2 pr + rt).
trick: r is a midpoint, so pr equals rv, and rv is rt plus tv — that is what fixes the ratio
why: Let tv = uw = k, so rt = su = 4k. Then rv = rt + tv = 5k, and since r is the midpoint of pv, pr = rv = 5k. The ratio is (4k + k + 4k) ⁄ (10k + 4k) = 9k ⁄ 14k = 9/14.
traps: A: used pr = 4k, forgetting the tv piece.
C: put 10k on top by counting rt twice.
D: cancelled the k and simplified 9/14 to a half by eye.

stem: The clock face below shows one minute of the minute hand's turn, marked x. Find x.
trick: one minute is a sixtieth of the whole turn, so 360 divided by 60
why: The minute hand goes right round in 60 minutes, so one minute is 360 ÷ 60 = 6°.
traps: A: divided 180 by 60.
B: divided 300 by 60, using only five of the six ten-minute blocks.
D: gave the angle for two minutes, or divided 720 by 60.

stem: Each square of the grid below is one unit across. What is the area of the rhombus, in square units?
trick: a rhombus is HALF the product of its diagonals, never base times height off the grid
why: The horizontal diagonal spans 12 units and the vertical one spans 8, so the area is ½ × 12 × 8 = 48.
traps: A: counted only the whole squares inside and ignored the half squares.
C: used a diagonal of 14 by counting grid lines instead of the gaps between them.
D: multiplied the diagonals without halving.

stem: A right triangle has hypotenuse 26 cm, and its legs are y and y + 14. Find its area, in cm².
trick: the legs differ by 14 and the hypotenuse is 26, which is the 10-24-26 triangle; the area uses the LEGS, never the hypotenuse
why: y² + (y + 14)² = 676 gives 2y² + 28y − 480 = 0, so y² + 14y − 240 = 0 and y = 10. The legs are 10 and 24, and the area is ½ × 10 × 24 = 120 cm².
traps: A: used ½ × 10 × 12.
B: used ½ × 26 × 6.5, treating the hypotenuse as a base.
D: multiplied the two legs without halving, then adjusted.

stem: Find the value of x in the figure below.
trick: the slant closes a right triangle whose horizontal leg is the DIFFERENCE of the two parallel sides
why: The horizontal leg is 19 − 11 = 8 and the vertical leg is 15, so x = √(64 + 225) = √289 = 17. This is the 8-15-17 triangle.
traps: A: took x as the height of 15.
B: rounded √289 badly, or used √(15² + 5²).
D: took x as the base of 19.

stem: A triangle has two sides of 7 cm and 11 cm. Which of the following CANNOT be the length of the third side, in cm?
trick: the third side must be strictly between the difference and the sum of the other two
why: The third side must satisfy 11 − 7 < s < 11 + 7, that is 4 < s < 18. 18 fails, because a side equal to the sum makes the three points collinear rather than a triangle.
traps: A: 5 is above 4, so it is allowed.
B: 9 sits comfortably inside the range.
C: 13 is below 18, so it is allowed.

stem: A regular octagon rests on a straight line as shown. Find x + y.
trick: each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360 divided by the number of sides — the interior angle is a detour
why: A regular octagon has interior angle 135°, so each exterior angle is 180 − 135 = 45°. Then x + y = 45 + 45 = 90°.
traps: B: used a hexagon's exterior angle of 60 twice.
C: gave one interior angle instead of two exterior ones.
D: added the two interior angles and subtracted from 540.

stem: In the figure, the two marked sides are equal and the two arrowed lines are parallel. Find x.
trick: get the base angle from the isosceles triangle first, then carry it across with corresponding angles
why: The triangle is isosceles with apex 40°, so each base angle is (180 − 40) ÷ 2 = 70°. The ray is parallel to the left-hand side, so x corresponds to that 70° base angle. x = 70°.
traps: A: copied the apex angle.
D: gave the angle on the other side of the line, 180 − 70.

stem: Find the value of x in the figure below.
trick: angles round a point add to 360, and the square is a right angle you have to remember to count
why: The three angles at the point fill a whole turn: 140 + 90 + x = 360, so x = 130°.
traps: B: subtracted from 340 rather than 360.
D: copied the given 140°.

stem: A small circle has radius 5 cm and a large circle has radius 9 cm. Which is greater?   A: three times the area of the small circle   B: the area of the large circle
trick: area scales with the SQUARE of the radius — compare 3 × 25 with 81, not 3 × 5 with 9
why: The small area is 25π and three times it is 75π. The large area is 81π. Since 75π < 81π, B is greater.
traps: A: compared 3 × 5 = 15 with 9 and stopped — that is the radius, not the area.
C: took 3 × 25 as 81 by rounding.
D: both radii are given, so both areas are determined; π cancels.

stem: The rectangle below is cut by the marked widths along the top. Find the ratio of the shaded region to the whole rectangle.
trick: a slanted strip is a parallelogram — its area is its top width times the height, exactly as if it stood upright
why: The shaded strip is a parallelogram of width 2 and full height, and the rectangle is 5 + 2 + 3 = 10 wide with the same height. So the ratio is 2 : 10 = 1 : 5.
traps: A: used the 5 and the 2 and read 2 : 8.
C: compared the strip with only the part of the rectangle to its left.
D: assumed the lean makes the strip bigger than an upright one of the same width.

stem: Tickets are numbered from 1 to 30. One is drawn at random. Find the probability that its number is a multiple of 5.
trick: probability is the favourable COUNT over the TOTAL, never the count on its own
why: The multiples of 5 up to 30 are 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 — six of them — so the probability is 6/30 = 1/5.
traps: B: counted only five multiples, forgetting that 30 is itself one.
C: counted the multiples of 3 instead, giving 10/30.
D: gave the COUNT of favourable tickets rather than a probability.

stem: A crate holds 40 oranges: 24 large and 16 small. In total 27 oranges are ripe, and 11 of the small ones are ripe. How many large oranges are unripe?
trick: 'large or small' and 'ripe or unripe' are two different cuts of the same 40 — build the table before answering
why: Ripe oranges number 27, of which 11 are small, so 16 are large and ripe. There are 24 large oranges altogether, so 24 − 16 = 8 large ones are unripe.
traps: A: subtracted 11 from 16 and stopped.
C: used 27 − 16 and then a wrong large total.
D: gave the number of unripe oranges of both sizes (40 − 27).

stem: In the Venn diagram below, which is greater?   A: the number of dots in P   B: the number of dots in Q and R
trick: 'in Q and R' means in BOTH — the overlap, not the total of the two
why: P holds 6 dots. 'In Q and R' means the overlap of Q and R, which holds 1. So A is greater. (The same skill without a picture reads: 10 employees in one section, 8 in the other, 15 people in total, so 10 + 8 − 15 = 3 are in both.)
traps: B: read 'Q and R' as the total of Q and R (5 + 3 = 8) and forgot that the shared dot is counted twice.
C: counted Q alone against a miscount of P.
D: every dot is visible, so nothing is missing.

stem: In the Venn diagram below, which is greater?   A: the number of dots in P   B: the number of dots in Q or R
trick: 'Q or R' is the union — count each dot once, even where the circles cross
why: P holds 6 dots. 'In Q or R' means in either, which is 5 + 3 − 1 = 7 dots. So B is greater. This is the same picture as the previous item; only the word between Q and R changes.
traps: A: repeated the answer to the previous item without re-reading the word 'or'.
C: counted the union as 6 by double-counting the shared dot.
D: every dot is visible.

stem: The chart shows overseas visitors to AlUla, in thousands. If 300 thousand domestic visitors came in 1447, find the domestic share of all visitors that year.
trick: the bar gives OVERSEAS visitors only; the total is that bar plus the domestic figure
why: The 1447 bar reads 1200 thousand from overseas. The total is 1200 + 300 = 1500 thousand, and 300 ⁄ 1500 = 1/5 = 20%.
traps: A: divided 300 by 2000 by misreading the bar.
C: used the 1446 bar of 1000 instead of the 1447 bar.
D: took the ratio of domestic to OVERSEAS (300 : 1200 = 25%) — and then mis-rounded.

stem: The bar chart below shows the sales of two branches. What is the ratio of the first branch to the second?
trick: read both bars off the axis, then divide; do not eyeball the ratio
why: The first branch reads 800 and the second 200, so the ratio is 800 : 200 = 4 : 1.
traps: A: wrote the ratio the wrong way round.
B: read the second bar as 400.
C: compared the two heights by eye rather than off the axis.

stem: The chart shows vehicles at four gates. To avoid delays caused by buses and lorries, which gate is the best?
trick: 'buses and lorries' means add those two bars only — the car bar is a decoy and must be ignored
why: Buses + lorries: Gate 1 is 40 + 50 = 90, Gate 2 is 55 + 40 = 95, Gate 3 is 30 + 35 = 65, Gate 4 is 45 + 60 = 105. Gate 3 is the lowest, so it is the best.
traps: A: added all three bars, which puts Gate 1 at 180 and hides Gate 3's advantage.
B: read 'best' as the busiest gate.
D: Gate 4 is the WORST on the two rows that matter.

stem: In the chart below, the average of Physics and Arabic equals which subject?
trick: the mean of two bars is the height halfway between them — find that height on the axis, then read across
why: Physics is 90 and Arabic is 30, so their average is 60 — the height of the Geography bar.
traps: A: English is 75, the average of Physics and Geography.
C: Art is 45, the average of Arabic and Geography.
D: Physics is one of the two bars being averaged, so it cannot be the answer.

stem: Four investment funds are plotted below across four years. Over 2022, 2023 and 2024 only one of them stayed clear of loss in every single year. Which one?
trick: read the window before reading the bars — 'the last three years' is 2022 to 2024, so a dip in 2021 does not count
why: The last three years are 2022, 2023 and 2024. Fund B dips in 2022, Fund C in 2023 and Fund D in 2024. Fund A is positive throughout that window; its only loss is in 2021, which is outside it.
traps: B: Fund B's loss falls inside the window.
C: Fund C has the tallest bar of all, which is not the same as never losing.
D: Fund D's loss is in the very last year — inside the window.

stem: The scatter graph below shows the readings taken in each quarter. Find the mean of the three readings plotted for the third quarter.
trick: 'third quarter' is the third GROUP of points, not the third point in each group
why: The third group reads 45, 55 and 50, and (45 + 55 + 50) ÷ 3 = 50.
traps: A: gave the lowest point in the group rather than the average.
C: gave the highest point in the group.
D: averaged the fourth group by mistake.

stem: The line graph below shows the monthly figures. Find the percentage increase from Rajab to Shaaban.
trick: percentage increase divides by the STARTING value, not by the finishing one
why: Rajab is 5 and Shaaban is 12. The increase is 7, and 7 ÷ 5 = 1.4, so 140%.
traps: A: divided the increase by 6 after misreading Rajab.
C: divided the increase by the average of the two values.
D: divided 12 by 5 and read 2.4 as 240% — that is the RATIO, not the increase.

stem: The chart below shows the cups sold each day. On which day is the number of tea and juice cups together double the number of coffee cups?
trick: add the two named bars first, then compare with DOUBLE the third — do not compare the bars one at a time
why: Thursday: 45 + 35 = 80, and 2 × 40 = 80. ✓  Friday: 30 + 45 = 75 against 100. Saturday: 50 + 30 = 80 against 120. Sunday: 40 + 50 = 90 against 60.
traps: B: Friday has the tallest coffee bar of the first three, which reads as 'the most' rather than 'double'.
C: Saturday's tea and juice also total 80, but its coffee bar is 60, not 40.
D: Sunday is the only other day where tea and juice beat coffee — but 90 is not 60 doubled.

stem: A press prints 150 pages in 6 minutes. How many minutes does it take to print 1000 pages?
trick: find the rate per minute first, then divide — the two given numbers never both go on the same side
why: The rate is 150 ÷ 6 = 25 pages per minute, so 1000 ÷ 25 = 40 minutes.
traps: A: used a rate of 33 pages per minute.
C: scaled 6 minutes by 1000/150 and rounded badly.
D: used a rate of 20 pages per minute.

stem: Three teams lay a pipeline. The first lays a third of it and the second lays half of it. The third team lays the remaining 24 m. How many metres does the second team lay?
trick: the leftover fraction is what fixes the whole — add the two given fractions and subtract from 1 first
why: The first two lay 1/3 + 1/2 = 5/6, so the third team's 24 m is the remaining sixth. The whole pipeline is 144 m, and the second team lays half of it, 72 m.
traps: A: took a third of 144.
B: found the total 144 and then took 24 × 2.5.
D: took two thirds of 144.

stem: Hessa's age is 4 times Reem's age, and Munira's age is 6 times Hessa's age. Which is greater?   A: Reem's age   B: Munira's age
trick: chain the multipliers: 4 then 6 is 24, not 10
why: Munira is 6 × 4 = 24 times Reem's age, so for any positive age Munira is older. B is greater.
traps: A: reversed the chain and made Reem the multiple.
C: assumed the two ends of the chain balance.
D: the multipliers fix the comparison without knowing any actual age.

stem: A cashier has 45 banknotes, an equal number of 10 SAR, 20 SAR and 100 SAR. Which is greater?   A: 2000 SAR   B: the total value of the notes
trick: an equal split of 45 into three kinds is 15 of each — the count per KIND is what you multiply by, not 45
why: Equal numbers means 15 notes of each, so the total is 15 × (10 + 20 + 100) = 15 × 130 = 1950 SAR. That is less than 2000, so A is greater.
traps: B: multiplied 45 by 130 instead of 15 by 130.
C: rounded 1950 up to 2000.
D: 'an equal number' fixes the split completely, so the total IS determined.

stem: A coach travels from Jeddah to Taif in 150 minutes. The distance is 200 km. Find its average speed.
trick: convert the minutes to hours BEFORE dividing, never after
why: 150 minutes is 2.5 hours, so the speed is 200 ÷ 2.5 = 80 km/h.
traps: B: divided 200 by 2.86 after a conversion slip.
D: used 3 hours' worth of distance over 2.5 hours.

stem: Hamad is south-east of Turki, and Bader is east of Hamad. Where is Turki in relation to Bader?
trick: reverse each bearing one step at a time; south-east reversed is north-west
why: Reverse the first bearing: Turki is north-west of Hamad. Bader is east of Hamad, so Turki is further west and further north of Bader — north-west.
traps: B: reversed only the south part and kept the east.
C: gave Bader's position relative to Turki instead of Turki's relative to Bader.
D: did not reverse the bearing at all.

stem: In a four-digit number, the digit 2 is next to the digit 9 and not next to the digit 4. The digit 9 is not next to the digit 4. The number is odd. Which number is it?
trick: the adjacency conditions eliminate the options before the odd-or-even rule is even needed
why: In 4129 the pair 2-9 is adjacent, 2 sits next to 1 and 9 only, 9 sits next to 2 only, and the number ends in 9 so it is odd. In 4291 the 4 touches the 2; in 1429 the 4 touches the 2; in 1294 the 9 touches the 4.
traps: A: 2 and 9 are adjacent, but 9 sits next to 4, and the number is even.
B: same — 2 and 9 are adjacent, but 4 sits next to 2.
D: checked only that 2 and 9 are adjacent.

stem: A household spends 1200 SAR a month on internet, electricity and water together. It spends 10 800 SAR a year on internet and electricity combined. How much does it spend per month on water?
trick: put both figures on the SAME period before subtracting — a year is twelve months
why: 10 800 a year is 10 800 ÷ 12 = 900 a month on internet and electricity, so water is 1200 − 900 = 300 SAR a month.
traps: A: divided the 900 between two items and subtracted only one share.
D: divided 10 800 by 10 and subtracted from 1200 wrongly.

stem: A workshop lasted 3 hours and 50 minutes and finished at 00:20. When did it start?
trick: work backwards from the finish time, and remember the clock passes midnight
why: Going back 3 hours from 00:20 gives 21:20, and back another 50 minutes gives 20:30.
traps: A: took off 4 hours 50 minutes.
B: took off 4 hours 20 minutes.
D: took off 3 hours 10 minutes.

stem: One shop sells dates at 12 SAR a kilogram, and for every 3 kg bought it gives 1 kg free. A second shop sells dates at 10 SAR a kilogram with no offer. A customer wants 8 kg. How much less does the cheaper shop cost, in SAR?
trick: buy 3 get 1 free means you pay for 3 of every 4 kilograms — count the paid kilograms, not the free ones
why: With 'buy 3 get 1 free', 8 kg comes as two blocks of 4, and the customer pays for 3 kg in each block — 6 kg in total, at 12 SAR each, which is 72 SAR. The second shop charges 8 × 10 = 80 SAR. The first shop is cheaper by 8 SAR.
traps: A: paid for 7 kg at the first shop by giving away only one kilogram in total.
C: paid for 8 kg at the first shop and compared 96 with 80 incorrectly.
D: compared 96 with 80.

stem: Riding at a steady pace, a cyclist needs 95 seconds for every lap. Which is greater?   A: the riding time for 13 laps   B: 20 minutes
trick: put both on the same unit before comparing — 1235 seconds against 1200 is only 35 seconds apart, so it has to be worked out, not estimated
why: 13 × 95 = 1235 seconds. 20 minutes is 20 × 60 = 1200 seconds. Since 1235 > 1200, A is greater.
traps: B: rounded 95 down to 90 and got 1170.
C: rounded 1235 to 1200 and called it a tie — this is the trap the item is built on.
D: the speed is constant and both figures are exact.

stem: The zakat due on a sum of money is 250 SAR. What is the original sum, in SAR?
trick: zakat is 2.5%, so the sum is the zakat divided by 0.025 — which is the same as multiplying by 40
traps: A: used a rate of 4%.
B: multiplied by 32.
D: multiplied by 50, using a rate of 2%.

stem: Sultan is standing in a queue. He is 9th from the front and 15th from the back. How many people are in the queue?
trick: add the two positions and subtract one — Sultan is counted in both
why: 9 + 15 = 24, but Sultan himself has been counted twice, so the queue holds 24 − 1 = 23 people.
traps: A: subtracted two instead of one.
C: added the two positions and forgot to subtract at all.
D: added one instead of subtracting.

stem: A parcel service charges 6 SAR for the first 2 kg and 75 halala for each extra kilogram. A customer paid 15 SAR. What was the parcel's weight, in kg?
trick: peel the fixed charge off first, and convert halala to riyals before dividing
why: 15 − 6 = 9 SAR is for the extra weight. At 0.75 SAR per kilogram that is 9 ÷ 0.75 = 12 extra kilograms, so the parcel weighs 2 + 12 = 14 kg.
traps: A: gave the extra weight and forgot the first 2 kg.
C: divided the full 15 SAR by 0.75 and then trimmed.
D: used 0.6 SAR per kilogram.

stem: A mother and her four children have ages summing to 94 years today. What will the five ages sum to in 6 years' time?
trick: every one of the five people gains the same 6 years, so the sum rises by 5 x 6, not by 6
why: Five people each gain 6 years, so the sum rises by 5 × 6 = 30. The new sum is 94 + 30 = 124.
traps: A: added 6 once.
B: added 6 three times.
C: added 6 four times, counting only the children.

stem: Noura has two brothers, Ziyad and Faris. Ziyad is 4 years younger than Noura and Faris is 8 years older than Noura. If the two brothers' ages add to 46, how old is Noura?
trick: the two offsets do not cancel — write both brothers in terms of Noura and collect them
traps: A: solved 2N + 8 = 46.
C: halved 46 and treated the offsets as cancelling.
D: solved 2N − 4 = 46.

stem: A bakery makes trays in a repeating order: date, cheese, pistachio, then almond, and starts again. What is tray number 63?
trick: divide by the length of the cycle and read the REMAINDER — a remainder of zero means the last item, not the first
why: The cycle has length 4, and 63 ÷ 4 = 15 remainder 3. A remainder of 3 is the third item in the cycle, pistachio.
traps: A: took a remainder of 3 as meaning three whole cycles and started again.
B: used a cycle of length 5.
D: took the remainder 3 to mean 'three from the end'.

stem: Two friends set off towards each other at the same moment, one walking at 5 km/h and the other cycling at 19 km/h. They meet after 45 minutes. How far apart were they to begin with, in km?
trick: when two things move towards each other, ADD the speeds and treat it as one journey
why: The gap closes at 5 + 19 = 24 km/h. In 45 minutes, which is 0.75 hours, that is 24 × 0.75 = 18 km.
traps: A: used the difference of the speeds instead of the sum.
B: used 24 km/h for 37.5 minutes.
D: forgot to convert 45 minutes and used a full hour.

stem: Bandar is taller than Yousef. Adel is taller than Salem but shorter than Yousef. Which is greater?   A: Bandar's height   B: Salem's height
trick: write the chain out in one line before answering — every link points the same way here
why: The chain is Bandar > Yousef > Adel > Salem, so Bandar is taller than Salem. A is greater.
traps: B: reversed the second sentence and put Adel above Yousef.
C: assumed two people not directly compared cannot be ordered.
D: the chain connects Bandar to Salem through Yousef and Adel, so it IS decidable.

stem: In an examination 120 students passed, and the number who failed was one quarter of the number who passed. How many students sat the examination?
trick: the fraction is of the PASSERS, not of the whole entry — work out the failures, then add
why: The failures number 120 ÷ 4 = 30, so the entry was 120 + 30 = 150.
traps: A: took a fifth of 120 and added.
C: treated 120 as three quarters of the entry.
D: treated 120 as two thirds of the entry.

stem: The table below is complete except for one figure. How many trainers are there in Jeddah?
trick: use the ROW that the gap sits in, not the column — the row total is the one that closes
why: The trainers row must add to 186, and 42 + 55 + 24 = 121, so the missing figure is 186 − 121 = 65. (The Jeddah column checks out too: 65 + 31 + 97 = 193.)
traps: A: closed the column with 193 − 31 − 97 and then slipped by six.
B: added the row wrongly as 124.
D: took the Abha column total instead of the missing cell.

stem: In the table below, which categories at least TREBLED between 1443 and 1447?
trick: test every row against the multiplier, and ignore the middle column — it is there to slow you down
why: Housing goes 40 → 120, exactly three times. Transport goes 25 → 75, exactly three times. Food goes 60 → 150, only two and a half times. Health goes 30 → 66, only 2.2 times. So Housing and Transport.
traps: A: Food rises the most in absolute terms (90) but not by the largest factor.
C: Transport qualifies, but so does Housing.
D: Health falls short at 2.2 times.

stem: A farm's harvest over six years totalled 1080 tons. The second and fifth years together produced 210 tons. Using the chart, find the angle of the fifth year's sector.
trick: convert tons to degrees ONCE — the whole 1080 tons is 360°, so every 3 tons is one degree
why: 1080 tons fill 360°, so 3 tons make 1°. The second and fifth years are 210 tons = 70°. The second year is marked 40°, so the fifth is 70 − 40 = 30°.
traps: A: gave 210 ÷ 3 ÷ 3 by dividing twice.
B: subtracted 40 from 65 after mis-converting.
D: used 105° for the pair by taking 2 tons to the degree.

stem: The chart shows how 480 trainees finished a course. How many passed?
trick: the passed sector is a straight line through the centre, so it is exactly half — no measuring needed
why: The 'Passed' sector is bounded by a diameter, so it is 180° of 360°, that is half. Half of 480 is 240.
traps: A: took a third.
B: used 150° instead of 180°.
D: added the absent sector to the passed one.

stem: In the pie chart below, find the angle of the sector for the trainees who failed.
trick: the three sectors fill a whole turn, so subtract from 360 — and remember the passed sector is 180, not something to measure
why: Passed is 180° and absent is 45°, so failed is 360 − 180 − 45 = 135°.
traps: A: subtracted 45 from 150.
B: forgot the 45° absent sector and took 360 − 180 − 60.
D: subtracted only the 45° and halved what was left.

stem: The circle below is divided into equal parts. Find the total angle of the shaded parts.
trick: count the parts in the WHOLE circle first, then the shaded ones — 360 divided by the count gives one part
why: There are 10 equal parts, so each is 360 ÷ 10 = 36°. Four are shaded, giving 4 × 36 = 144°.
traps: A: counted three shaded parts.
B: divided 360 by 10 and multiplied by 3.5.
D: divided 360 by 9 and multiplied by 4.

stem: Eight equal circles are drawn in a row along the diameter of a large circle, as shown. Find the ratio of the area of one small circle to the area of the large circle.
trick: the eight small DIAMETERS make up the large diameter, so the radii are in the ratio 1 : 8 — and areas square that
why: Eight small diameters span 80 cm, so each small circle has diameter 10 and radius 5. The large radius is 40. The areas are in the ratio 5² : 40² = 25 : 1600 = 1 : 64.
traps: A: gave the ratio of the radii, not the areas.
B: squared 4 instead of 8.
D: used the diameter 80 against the small radius 5 without squaring.

stem: The areas of two circles are in the ratio shown. Find the ratio of their radii.
trick: area scales with the SQUARE of the radius, so go backwards by taking the square root
why: If the areas are 1 : 196 then the radii are √1 : √196 = 1 : 14.
traps: B: halved 196 twice.
C: halved 196 once.
D: repeated the area ratio without taking the root.

stem: In the figure, which is greater?   A: m(P) + m(Q)   B: 135°
trick: an exterior angle equals the two remote interior angles ADDED — the 55° is a decoy you never need
why: The exterior angle at R is 130°, and an exterior angle equals the sum of the two opposite interior angles, so m(P) + m(Q) = 130°. That is less than 135°, so B is greater. (The 55° is not needed at all.)
traps: A: worked out m(Q) = 75 and then added 75 + 65 or similar.
C: read 130 as 135.
D: the exterior angle fixes the sum exactly.

stem: The shaded squares in the figure are 20% of all the squares in it. How many squares are there altogether?
trick: count the shaded squares first, then divide by the percentage — do not try to count the empty ones
why: The shaded block is 3 rows of 4, so 12 squares. If 12 is 20%, the total is 12 ÷ 0.20 = 60.
traps: A: divided 12 by 0.25.
B: multiplied 12 by 4.5.
D: divided 12 by 1/6 instead of 1/5.

stem: Five dates weigh the same as two figs, and five dates also weigh the same as four apricots. What weight of dates matches 24 figs together with 40 apricots?
trick: convert each fruit to dates SEPARATELY and add at the end — the two rates are different
why: Two figs are 5 dates, so 24 figs are 12 × 5 = 60 dates. Four apricots are 5 dates, so 40 apricots are 10 × 5 = 50 dates. Together, 60 + 50 = 110 dates.
traps: A: used the fig rate for both fruits.
B: used the apricot rate for both fruits.
D: added 24 and 40 first and then applied one rate.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: put everything on ONE base first — 25 is 5², so both brackets are powers of 5 and the exponents simply add
why: (5²)^(−2) = 5^(−4). And (25^(−1))^(−3) = 25³ = (5²)³ = 5⁶. Multiplying: 5^(−4) × 5⁶ = 5² = 25. That is exactly B, so they are equal.
traps: A: multiplied the two negative exponents to get a positive and overshot.
B: read 25³ as 5³.
D: both sides are explicit numbers.

stem: Find the value of the expression below.
trick: a cube root IS the power one third, so the two exponents add to a whole one
why: The cube root of 1/8 is (1/8)^(1/3). Multiplying by (1/8)^(2/3) adds the exponents: 1/3 + 2/3 = 1, so the answer is 1/8.
traps: A: took the cube root of 1/8 as 1/2 and stopped.
B: multiplied the exponents instead of adding them.
D: subtracted the exponents to get zero.

stem: Which quantity is greater?
trick: the two look like mirror images but they are not — a third of twelve is nothing like a twelfth of three
why: One third of 12 is 4. One twelfth of 3 is 0.25. So A is greater, by a long way.
traps: B: read the second as twelve thirds.
C: assumed swapping the numbers must give the same answer — this is the trap the item is built on.
D: both are explicit numbers.

stem: A generator's fuel lasts 9 hours when the load is full. How many hours will the same fuel last at 60% of that load?
trick: less load means MORE hours — divide by the fraction, never multiply by it
why: The fuel is fixed, so hours and load are inversely proportional: 9 ÷ 0.60 = 15 hours.
traps: A: multiplied 9 by 4/3.
C: doubled 9.
D: multiplied 9 by 60/25.

stem: A storage room holds 54 m³. How many boxes of 0.045 m³ each fit inside it?
trick: clear the decimal first — 54 ÷ 0.045 is the same as 54000 ÷ 45
traps: A: divided by 0.06.
B: divided by 0.05.
D: divided by 0.04.

stem: Sara paid 15% less than Huda for the same course. Between them they paid 5550 SAR. How much did Huda pay, in SAR?
trick: the 15% is off HUDA's price, so the total is 1.85 of it — halving 5550 is the trap
why: Sara paid 0.85 of Huda's price, so together they paid 1.85 × Huda = 5550, giving Huda = 3000 SAR.
traps: A: took 15% off half the total.
B: halved 5550 — which would only be right if they paid the same.
D: divided by 1.75.

stem: Find the value of x.
trick: both sides have the shape 'a number plus its reciprocal partner' — match the shapes instead of clearing denominators
why: The left side is 7/(x−2) + (x−2)/7 and the right is 7/11 + 11/7. They match when x − 2 = 11, so x = 13.
traps: A: solved x − 2 = 7.
B: gave the value of x − 2 instead of x.
D: added 2 to 13 a second time.

stem: Simplify the expression below.

stem: Ali has 240 SAR and saves 5 SAR a day. Ahmed has 100 SAR and saves 12 SAR a day. After how many days will they have the same amount?

D: used 8 cuts.

stem: A driver goes from Jeddah to Makkah at 60 km/h and returns along the same road at 40 km/h. What is the average speed for the whole journey, in km/h?
trick: the average of the two speeds is WRONG — the slow leg takes longer, so it weighs more; use twice their product over their sum
why: For equal distances the average speed is 2v₁v₂⁄(v₁ + v₂) = 2 × 60 × 40 ÷ 100 = 48 km/h. Not 50.
traps: A: took a rough three quarters of 60.
C: averaged the two speeds — the trap this item exists for.
D: averaged and then adjusted upward.

stem: A price rises by 20% and then falls by 20%. What is the overall change?
trick: the rise and the fall are taken on DIFFERENT amounts, so they do not cancel — the net is a + b + ab/100
traps: A: cancelled the two 20s, which is the trap.
C: got the size right but the direction wrong — a rise then a fall always ends lower.
D: subtracted the second 20% from the original price.

stem: In the triangle shown, AD bisects the angle at A. Find the length of DC, in centimetres.
trick: the bisector cuts the opposite side in the ratio of the two sides BESIDE the angle, not in half
why: BD⁄DC = AB⁄AC, so 6⁄DC = 9⁄15. Then DC = 6 × 15 ÷ 9 = 10 cm.
traps: A: matched BD to the wrong side, using 6 × 9 ÷ 15 and rounding.
C: assumed the bisector also bisects BC, doubling 6.
D: copied AC straight down as the answer.

stem: The four vertices of the quadrilateral shown lie on the circle. Find the size of the angle marked y.
trick: on a circle, OPPOSITE angles of the quadrilateral add to 180° — the two angles side by side tell you nothing
why: y is opposite the 78° angle, so y = 180° − 78° = 102°.
traps: A: subtracted from 146° instead of 180°.
B: copied the opposite angle, treating them as equal.
D: subtracted the adjacent 68° from 180° instead.

stem: A circular fountain rim at King Abdullah Park has radius 21 m. A path runs along the rim through a central angle of 120°. How long is the path? (Take π = 22⁄7.)
trick: an arc is a FRACTION of the circumference — the fraction is the angle over 360, and the circumference uses 2πr, not πr
why: The full circumference is 2 × 22⁄7 × 21 = 132 m. The path is 120⁄360 = one third of it, so 44 m.
traps: A: took a third of πr instead of 2πr.
C: took half the circumference instead of a third.
D: took two thirds, reading 120° as the part left over.

stem: A surveyor marks two points on a plan at (−3, 4) and (9, −1). How far apart are they?
trick: square the two GAPS, add, then take the root — the gap is a subtraction, so a negative coordinate widens it
why: The horizontal gap is 9 − (−3) = 12 and the vertical gap is 4 − (−1) = 5. Then √(144 + 25) = √169 = 13.
traps: A: used the horizontal gap alone.
C: added the two gaps, 12 + 5, and then subtracted 2.
D: added the two gaps.

stem: The equation below describes a circle. What is its radius?
trick: the number on the right is r SQUARED — and the centre reads with the signs flipped
why: Comparing with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² gives r² = 49, so r = 7. (The centre is (4, −3).)
traps: A: took the root of the 9 inside the bracket.
C: halved 49, confusing radius with diameter.
D: read 49 as the radius itself — the trap this item exists for.

stem: In the figure the two horizontal lines are parallel. Find the value of x.
trick: co-interior angles on the SAME side of the transversal add to 180°; only alternate and corresponding angles are equal
why: The two marked angles are co-interior, so (3x + 10) + (5x + 10) = 180, giving 8x = 160 and x = 20.
traps: A: set the two expressions equal, treating them as alternate angles.
C: added to 200 instead of 180.
D: solved 6x = 180, dropping both constants.

stem: In the figure the two triangles stand on the same base PQ, and the dashed line through R and S is parallel to PQ. Which is greater?   A: the area of triangle PQR   B: the area of triangle PQS
trick: area depends on the base and the PERPENDICULAR height only — a triangle that leans is not larger, and between parallels every apex has the same height
why: Both triangles have base PQ and the same height, because R and S sit on a line parallel to PQ. The areas are equal.
traps: A: judged by the longer sloping sides of PQR.
B: judged by S sitting further along.
D: the parallel line fixes the height, so this is decidable.

stem: A square is drawn so that the number giving its area is equal to the number giving its perimeter. What is the length of one side?
trick: write both as expressions in the side and solve — do not hunt for the answer by trying values
why: s² = 4s, so s² − 4s = 0 and s(s − 4) = 0. A side cannot be 0, so s = 4. (Area 16, perimeter 16.)
traps: A: solved s = 4 ÷ 2.
C: doubled the correct side.
D: gave the area rather than the side.

stem: A circular tile is set inside a square panel as shown below, touching all four sides. The panel has side 14 cm. Find the shaded area, in square centimetres. (Take π = 22⁄7.)
trick: the circle's DIAMETER equals the side of the square, so the radius is half of it — halve before you square
why: The radius is 7 cm. Square 14² = 196; circle 22⁄7 × 49 = 154. Shaded = 196 − 154 = 42 cm².
traps: A: used a radius of 14 and then patched the negative answer.
C: doubled the correct difference.
D: gave the area of the circle rather than what is left.

stem: Two equal circles are fitted inside the rectangle shown so that each touches three sides and the two touch each other. Find the shaded area, in square centimetres. (Take π = 3.14.)
trick: the height of the rectangle fixes the radius, and the length is then FOUR radii — subtract two circles, not one
why: The height 6 cm is one diameter, so r = 3 and the length 12 = 4r checks out. Shaded = 12 × 6 − 2 × 3.14 × 3² = 72 − 56.52 = 15.48 cm².
traps: B: subtracted only one circle.
C: used a radius of 1.5, halving twice.
D: gave the area of the two circles instead of what is left.

stem: A square and a circle are each made from 24 cm of wire, with none left over. Which is greater?   A: the area enclosed by the square   B: the area enclosed by the circle
trick: for a fixed perimeter the CIRCLE always encloses the most — the more corners a shape loses, the more it holds
why: The square has side 6 and area 36 cm². The circle has 2πr = 24, so r ≈ 3.82 and area ≈ 45.8 cm². B is greater.
traps: A: assumed the straight-sided shape holds more.
C: assumed equal perimeter forces equal area — the trap this item exists for.
D: both perimeters are given, so both areas are fixed.

stem: Two similar triangular sails have corresponding sides in the ratio 3 : 5. The smaller sail has area 45 m². What is the area of the larger one, in square metres?
trick: areas scale by the SQUARE of the side ratio — 3 : 5 on the sides is 9 : 25 on the areas
traps: A: scaled by 5⁄3 once instead of squaring.
B: used the ratio 9 : 25 upside down and rounded.
D: tripled the smaller area.

stem: A triangular flowerbed has area 84 m² and a perpendicular height of 12 m. How long is its base, in metres?
trick: working backwards means DOUBLING the area first — the half in the formula moves to the other side
traps: A: divided 84 by 12 and then halved.
B: read the height back as the base.
D: doubled the correct base, halving nothing.

stem: How many rectangles of any size can be traced along the lines of the grid shown?
trick: a rectangle is fixed by choosing TWO of the vertical lines and TWO of the horizontal ones — count lines, not squares
why: There are 4 vertical lines and 3 horizontal ones. Choosing 2 of each gives 6 × 3 = 18 rectangles.
traps: A: counted only the six unit squares.
B: counted the unit squares and the six 1 × 2 rectangles.
D: counted every pair of lines including repeats.

stem: A storage box measures 8 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm. Which is greater?   A: its volume in cubic centimetres   B: its total surface area in square centimetres
trick: surface area needs all THREE pairs of faces — 2(lw + lh + wh), not four sides like a room
why: Volume = 8 × 5 × 3 = 120. Surface = 2(40 + 24 + 15) = 158. So B is greater.
traps: A: counted only four faces, giving 118.
C: no pair of these figures is equal.
D: all three dimensions are given, so both are fixed.

stem: A cylindrical water tank has radius 7 m and height 10 m. What is its volume, in cubic metres? (Take π = 22⁄7.)
trick: the base is a CIRCLE, so square the radius before multiplying by the height — πr²h, never 2πrh
traps: A: used the circumference 2πr and forgot the height.
B: used the curved surface area 2πrh instead of the volume.
D: doubled the volume, using 2πr²h.

stem: A rooftop tank measures 2 m by 1.5 m by 0.8 m. How many litres does it hold when full?
trick: one cubic metre is a THOUSAND litres — the metre-to-centimetre factor of 100 is cubed, not used once
why: The volume is 2 × 1.5 × 0.8 = 2.4 m³, and 2.4 × 1000 = 2400 litres.
traps: A: gave the volume in cubic metres times ten.
B: multiplied by 100 instead of 1000.
D: multiplied by 10 000.

stem: Ten teachers meet at a staff breakfast. Which is greater?   A: the number of handshakes if each pair shakes hands once   B: the number of gifts if each teacher gives a gift to every other teacher
trick: a handshake is SHARED by the pair but a gift has a giver and a receiver — one is n(n−1)/2, the other is n(n−1)
why: Handshakes: 10 × 9 ÷ 2 = 45. Gifts: 10 × 9 = 90, because A giving to B is not the same as B giving to A. B is greater.
traps: A: counted the gifts as pairs too.
C: treated the two situations as the same counting problem — the trap this item exists for.
D: the number of teachers fixes both counts.

stem: A bicycle wheel has diameter 70 cm. How many complete turns does it make over 4.4 km? (Take π = 22⁄7.)
trick: one turn covers one CIRCUMFERENCE — and the units must meet, so put the distance into centimetres first
why: Circumference = 22⁄7 × 70 = 220 cm. The distance is 4.4 km = 440 000 cm. Then 440 000 ÷ 220 = 2000 turns.
traps: A: used the diameter as the distance per turn and rounded.
C: used the radius 35 cm in place of the circumference.
D: divided by 22 instead of 220.

stem: A shop in Jeddah sells a jacket for 621 SAR, making a profit of 15% on what it paid. What did the shop pay, in SAR?
trick: the percentage is taken on the COST, which is the unknown — so divide by 1.15; taking 15% off the selling price is the trap
traps: A: took 15% off 621 — the trap this item exists for.
C: subtracted 15% of 540 rather than working back to it.
D: subtracted a flat 15 SAR.

stem: A prize of 3600 SAR is divided between three students in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7. How much more does the largest share get than the smallest, in SAR?
trick: find the value of ONE part first — the total is 12 parts here, not 3
why: There are 2 + 3 + 7 = 12 parts, so one part is 3600 ÷ 12 = 300 SAR. The difference is 7 − 2 = 5 parts, or 1500 SAR.
traps: A: used the difference 3 parts between the two smaller shares.
B: divided the total by 3 and took a quarter.
D: gave the largest share instead of the difference.

stem: One painter can finish a wall in 12 hours and a second can finish the same wall in 6 hours. Working together, how many hours do they take?
trick: add the RATES, not the times — and the answer must be shorter than the faster worker alone, which rules the average out
why: In one hour they paint 1⁄12 + 1⁄6 = 3⁄12 = 1⁄4 of the wall, so the whole wall takes 4 hours.
traps: A: halved the faster time.
C: gave the faster painter's own time.
D: averaged 12 and 6 — the trap this item exists for.

stem: Today is Tuesday. What day of the week will it be 100 days from now?
trick: only the REMAINDER after dividing by 7 moves the day — the whole weeks in between change nothing
why: 100 ÷ 7 = 14 remainder 2, so the day moves forward 2 from Tuesday, to Thursday.
traps: A: moved forward 1, using a remainder of 1.
C: moved forward 3.
D: counted 100 ÷ 7 as 14 remainder 4.

stem: Eight students are available. Which is greater?   A: the number of ways to pick 3 of them for a committee   B: the number of ways to pick 3 of them for first, second and third place in a race
trick: ask whether ORDER changes the outcome — on a committee it does not, on a podium it does, and ordering multiplies by 3! = 6
why: Committee: 8 × 7 × 6 ÷ 6 = 56. Podium: 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. B is greater, by a factor of 6.
traps: A: divided the podium count by 6 as well.
C: treated the two as the same selection — the trap this item exists for.
D: eight students and three places fix both counts.

stem: Section A has 20 students with a mean mark of 78. Section B has 30 students with a mean mark of 68. What is the mean mark of all 50 students?
trick: the two means cannot simply be averaged — the bigger group pulls harder, so add the TOTAL marks and divide by the total number of students
traps: A: leaned too far towards the larger, weaker group.
C: averaged 78 and 68 — the trap this item exists for.
D: weighted the sections the wrong way round.

stem: A student's first four test marks are 82, 76, 90 and 68. What must the fifth mark be for the mean of all five to be exactly 80?
trick: the mean tells you the TOTAL — five marks averaging 80 must add to 400, so the missing mark is what is left
why: The five marks must total 5 × 80 = 400. The first four total 316, so the fifth is 400 − 316 = 84.
traps: A: averaged the four marks given, 79, and stopped there.
B: adjusted the mean of the four by two marks.
D: made the total 404.

stem: In a class of 20 students, 6 scored 5 marks, 9 scored 7 marks, 4 scored 8 marks and 1 scored 10 marks. What is the mean mark?
trick: each mark must be counted as many times as it OCCURS — divide by the number of students, never by the number of different marks
traps: A: rounded the total down before dividing.
C: gave the most common mark instead of the mean.
D: averaged the four different marks, (5+7+8+10)÷4 — the trap this item exists for.

stem: The seven values 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 14 are recorded, and then the 14 is corrected to 70. Which is greater?   A: the increase in the mean   B: the increase in the median
trick: one extreme value drags the MEAN and leaves the median where it is — the median only counts positions, not sizes
why: The mean rises from 56⁄7 = 8 to 112⁄7 = 16, an increase of 8. The median is the fourth value, 8, both before and after, so it does not move at all.
traps: B: assumed a bigger value must pull every average up.
C: assumed the two averages always move together.
D: every value is given, so both averages are fixed.

stem: A bag holds 24 marbles, of which 9 are green. One marble is taken at random. What is the probability that it is NOT green?
trick: subtract from the WHOLE first — 24 − 9 = 15 favourable outcomes, and the denominator stays at 24
why: There are 24 − 9 = 15 marbles that are not green, so the probability is 15⁄24 = 5⁄8.
traps: A: gave the probability that it IS green.
C: divided the greens by the non-greens.
D: rounded 15⁄24 to 2⁄3.

stem: One of the numbers from 1 to 30 is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is a multiple of 3 or a multiple of 5?
trick: the numbers counted TWICE must come off once — 15 and 30 are multiples of both, so subtract them
why: Multiples of 3: 10. Multiples of 5: 6. Multiples of 15: 2, counted in both lists. So 10 + 6 − 2 = 14 numbers, and 14⁄30 = 7⁄15.
traps: B: added 10 and 6 without removing the overlap — the trap this item exists for.
C: counted 15 numbers.
D: counted 18 numbers.

stem: A box holds 5 red pens and 3 blue pens. Two pens are taken out one after the other, and the first is not put back. What is the probability that both are red?
trick: the second draw happens on a SMALLER box — both the top and the bottom of the second fraction go down by one
traps: B: reduced the total but not the reds.
C: multiplied 5⁄8 by 5⁄8, as if the pen were put back — the trap this item exists for.
D: halved the correct answer.

stem: At an exhibition in Jeddah the probability that a visitor buys a ticket for the evening show is 0.15. Out of 2400 visitors, how many would you expect to buy one?
trick: an expected number is just the probability TIMES the total — 0.15 is 15 per hundred, not 15 per thousand
traps: A: used 0.10.
B: used 1⁄8 of the visitors.
D: rounded 0.15 up to one sixth.

stem: A square board of side 14 cm carries a circular target of radius 7 cm that touches all four sides. A dart lands at a random point on the board. What is the probability that it lands on the target? (Take π = 22⁄7.)
trick: when the outcome is a position rather than a count, probability is an AREA over an area
traps: A: gave the probability of missing the target.
B: compared the radius with the side instead of the areas.
D: compared 7 with 8.

stem: A locker code is made of 2 letters chosen from A, B, C, D, E followed by 3 digits chosen from 0 to 9. Letters and digits may be repeated. How many different codes are possible?
trick: when repeats are allowed every position has the FULL set to choose from, and the positions multiply
traps: A: used only one letter position.
C: added the letter choices instead of multiplying them.

stem: A committee of 3 is chosen from 5 boys and 4 girls, and it must contain exactly 2 boys and 1 girl. In how many ways can it be formed?
trick: choose within each group SEPARATELY and then multiply — order does not matter on a committee
why: Boys: 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10 ways. Girls: 4 ways. Together 10 × 4 = 40.
traps: A: chose the boys in order and then halved twice.
C: counted the boys as ordered pairs, 20 × 4 ÷ 2 slipped.
D: ignored the condition and chose any 3 from 9 — the trap this item exists for.

stem: Find the median of 6, 13, 9, 20, 18, 11, 15 and 24.
trick: order the list first, and with an EVEN count the median is the average of the two middle values, not either one of them
why: In order: 6, 9, 11, 13, 15, 18, 20, 24. The two middle values are 13 and 15, so the median is (13 + 15) ÷ 2 = 14.
traps: A: took the fourth value on its own.
C: averaged the wrong pair.
D: took the fifth value on its own.

stem: The values 12, 19, 25, 31 and 47 are recorded, and then a sixth value of 8 is added. Which is greater?   A: the range of the first five values   B: the range of all six values
trick: the range depends only on the LARGEST and the SMALLEST — a new value changes it only if it falls outside both
why: First five: 47 − 12 = 35. All six: 47 − 8 = 39. So B is greater.
traps: A: assumed extra data cannot widen the range.
C: assumed a value inside the old maximum leaves the range alone — 8 is below the old minimum.
D: all six values are given.

stem: The pie chart below shows how a monthly household budget of 7200 SAR is divided. How much is spent on the part marked with a question mark, in SAR?
trick: two steps, and the first is the one that gets skipped — find the missing PERCENTAGE from 100 before touching the money
why: The three sectors given are 20 + 15 + 25 = 60%, so the missing one is 40%. Then 40% of 7200 = 2880 SAR.
traps: A: used 30% for the missing sector.
C: split what was left equally between two sectors and took half.
D: spent the 60% that IS labelled instead of the 40% that is not.

stem: The graph shows monthly sales at two branches. In which month is the difference between the branches greatest?
trick: the widest gap is not where either line PEAKS — read the vertical distance between the lines, month by month
why: The gaps are 8, 16, 4, 24 and 6. The largest, 24, is in April.
traps: A: read the month where the lower line first rises sharply.
B: read the month where the lines come closest.
D: read the month where the upper line ends, not where the gap is widest.

stem: The bar chart below shows quarterly sales, in thousands of SAR. By what percentage did sales rise from the third quarter to the fourth?
trick: a percentage rise is measured against the STARTING bar, so divide the rise by the third quarter, not by the fourth
traps: A: read the rise of 18 as 18% — the trap this item exists for.
B: divided the rise by the fourth quarter, 18 ÷ 63.
D: compared the fourth quarter with the first.

stem: The chart shows the times taken by 48 competitors, in minutes. Which interval contains the median time?
trick: the median sits at the MIDDLE POSITION, so add the bars up from the left until you pass half the total — the tallest bar is a different question
why: Half of 48 is 24. The running totals are 9, 21, 29, 43, 48, so the 24th and 25th values both fall in 20 – 30.
traps: A: stopped one interval early, at a running total of 21.
C: picked the tallest bar — the trap this item exists for.
D: picked the last interval.

stem: The table shows applicant numbers at four campuses. Which campus had the largest percentage increase from 1446 to 1447?
trick: the largest RISE and the largest percentage rise are rarely the same campus — always divide by the starting figure
why: Jeddah 48⁄240 = 20%, Makkah 54⁄180 = 30%, Madinah 12⁄120 = 10%, Dammam 21⁄60 = 35%. Dammam is largest.
traps: A: picked the campus with the largest numbers.
B: picked the largest rise in applicants, +54 — the trap this item exists for.
C: divided by the later figure instead of the earlier one.

stem: The chart shows the number of boys and girls at three schools. At which school or schools do girls make up more than half the students?
trick: compare each part with the WHOLE bar, not with the bar beside it — and 'more than half' does not include exactly half
why: A: 80 girls of 200, B: 110 of 200, C: 150 of 300. Only School B is above half; School C is exactly half.
traps: A: compared the girls' blocks with each other and picked the shortest bar.
C: counted School C, where the two parts are equal — the trap this item exists for.
D: picked the tallest bar.

stem: The pictogram below shows how many books were borrowed each week. How many more books were borrowed in week 2 than in week 3?
trick: count the symbols, then multiply by what ONE symbol is worth — the difference in symbols is not the difference in books
why: Week 2 has 7 symbols and week 3 has 4, a difference of 3 symbols. Each symbol is 8 books, so 3 × 8 = 24 books.
traps: A: gave the difference in symbols — the trap this item exists for.
B: used 2 books per symbol.
D: used the week 2 total, 7 × 8 ÷ 1.75.

stem: The shape below is made of horizontal and vertical sides only. Find its perimeter, in centimetres.
trick: slide every step out to the enclosing rectangle — the horizontal pieces add to the full width and the vertical pieces to the full height, so no missing side ever needs to be found
why: The horizontal sides total 2 × 7 = 14 cm and the vertical sides total 2 × 5 = 10 cm. The perimeter is 24 cm — the same as the 7 by 5 rectangle that encloses it.
traps: A: one width and one height added, 7 + 5.
B: the three visible steps counted instead of the full width.
D: the area of the enclosing rectangle given.

stem: The three angles of a triangle are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5. Find the largest angle.
trick: the parts share 180°, not 100° — divide 180 by the TOTAL number of parts before touching any option
why: 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 parts, so one part is 180 ÷ 12 = 15°. The largest angle is 5 × 15 = 75°.
traps: A: the smallest angle given.
B: the middle angle given.
D: a right angle assumed because 3 : 4 : 5 names a right triangle's SIDES — the trap this item exists for.

stem: A circle of the area shown is drawn inside a square so that it touches all four sides. Find the area of the square, in square centimetres.
trick: run the chain the whole way — area to radius to DIAMETER to side. The side of the square is twice the radius, and stopping at the radius is where the mark goes
why: πr² = 36π gives r = 6 cm. The circle touches all four sides, so the side of the square is the diameter, 12 cm, and the area is 12² = 144 cm².
traps: A: the circle's area copied as the square's.
B: the area doubled instead of the radius.
D: the side taken as the radius, 6, and then π left in by mistake.

stem: The triangle drawn in the circle below is right-angled, and its two shorter sides are 6 cm and 8 cm. Find the circumference of the circle. (Take π = 3.14.)
trick: a right angle drawn on a circle always stands on a DIAMETER — so the hypotenuse is the diameter, and Pythagoras hands you the whole circle
why: 6² + 8² = 100, so the hypotenuse is 10 cm. That hypotenuse is the diameter, so the circumference is 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 cm.
traps: A: the radius used where the diameter belongs.
C: 2πd used instead of πd.
D: the AREA of the circle given, 3.14 × 5².

stem: Use the statement below to find the value asked for.
trick: a square is never negative, so two squares can only add to zero if BOTH are zero — there is nothing to solve once you see that
why: x² ≥ 0 and y² ≥ 0 for all real numbers, so x² + y² = 0 forces x = 0 and y = 0. Then x² − y² = 0.
traps: A: a guess from the pattern of the other options.
B: the difference of squares expanded and a value invented for it.
C: x and y treated as opposites with non-zero values.

stem: Solve for x, given that x is positive.
trick: equal fractions with 1 on top mean equal bottoms — then write the number as a POWER that matches, and the exponents come off. An EVEN power allows a negative root too, which is why the question fixes the sign
why: (x + 8)⁴ = 10 000 = 10⁴, so x + 8 = ±10. The positive case gives x = 2. (The other case, x + 8 = −10, gives x = −18, which the condition rules out — an even power always carries that second root.)
traps: A: the 8 added instead of subtracted.
C: 10 000 read as 10³.
D: x + 8 taken as 14.

stem: Solve for x.
trick: if two fractions with 1 on top are equal then their bottoms are equal — cross-multiplying works but costs you twenty seconds you do not have
traps: A: both constants moved with the wrong sign.
C: 2x − x read as 3x.
D: the right-hand side doubled while cross-multiplying.

stem: Find the value of the product below.
